text:
Ask a model the same question twice, and you can get two different answers. Both sound sure of themselves. Only one matches the refund policy. Somebody has to decide which version of the feature ships, and that's a measurement problem. The statistics are ones you already know: sampling error, agreement, power, bias. What's new is that the output is text, it changes from run to run, and another model often grades it. This page has nine questions. Seven get worked through with real arithmetic, and two take a sentence each.

Question one. How have data scientist interviews changed with AI, artificial intelligence? The core loop hasn't: statistics, experiments, SQL and product sense. What's layered on top, mostly at mid and senior levels, is evaluating features built on a large language model, an LLM. Experimenting on AI features, where the treatment is itself random. Checking code and analysis an assistant wrote. And rounds where AI is allowed, or banned. Ask the recruiter, round by round. The rest of the page is about the first of those.

Question two. How would you measure the quality of an LLM feature, like drafted support replies? Start from the decision, not the metric. Agree on what a good reply is: correct, complete, on policy, the right tone. Then turn that into a rubric, pass or fail on each. Sample real traffic, split by intent and difficulty, so the rare cases are in it. Have experts label a subset, with two raters on some items, to see how much humans agree. Score every version on the same items. And report the uncertainty, because a pass rate with no interval invites people to ship noise. That last step is where most eval sets come up short.
